strengths: The paper addresses an important problem and presents an intuitive integration of LLM generation, chemistry-inspired rules, evolutionary memory, and property predictors.
The evaluation spans 14 nominal application areas and reports hit rate, stability, Pareto fronts, memorization, convergence, and several component ablations.
Including both successful and failed candidates in a multi-island memory is a reasonable mechanism for balancing exploitation and exploration.

The manuscript is generally readable and contains useful diagrams, prompts, algorithmic pseudocode, and predictor mappings. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/2c2b3ec2dcb14f9e80b4a7b65622d054/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central evaluation is circular: LLEMA optimizes predictions from Materials Project lookups and fixed CGCNN/ALIGNN surrogates, and success is then measured using the same oracle. Adaptive search can exploit surrogate errors, especially far out of distribution. There is no independent DFT recalculation, higher-fidelity simulation, held-out oracle, or experimental validation of the proposed structures.

Consequently, the claims of thermodynamic stability, synthesizability, physical realizability, and globally optimal Pareto trade-offs are unsupported. A predicted energy above hull is not evidence of synthesizability, and a nondominated front over a finite surrogate-scored sample is neither the true nor global Pareto frontier.

The paper does not establish that LLM-produced CIFs are physically meaningful. It provides no rigorous structural-validity checks, relaxation, charge-neutrality or oxidation-state validation, minimum-distance checks, symmetry analysis, or uncertainty/OOD filtering. Applying pretrained graph models to arbitrary unrelaxed CIFs can yield meaningless yet high-scoring predictions.

The benchmark is internally inconsistent. Several constraints in Table 1 differ materially from Appendix B: photovoltaic thresholds, hard-coating objectives, and aerospace constraints all change. The appendix even permits aerospace energy above hull up to 5 eV/atom, which is not a meaningful stability requirement. It is therefore unclear what was actually evaluated.

The property oracle is inadequately validated for the claimed tasks. No predictor errors, calibration, domain coverage, temperature or carrier-concentration conditions, or uncertainty estimates are reported. Directional dielectric and maximum piezoelectric checkpoints are treated as task-level scalar properties, while electrical conductivity is inferred from power factor and Seebeck coefficient without enough physical or unit details.

Baseline comparisons are not convincing. Unconditional models with default parameters are compared against an adaptive optimizer explicitly receiving the evaluation signal; G-SchNet is primarily a molecular generator; task conditioning and validity handling are insufficiently documented; and the arbitrary 10× sample allowance does not establish budget fairness. There are no repeated runs, uncertainty intervals, or significance tests.

Key definitions and results are inconsistent or incomplete. The normalized reward function is never specified; weights are described as equal, then unequal and manually curated; the handling of partially satisfying candidates differs between the prose and algorithm; and Table 3 reports stability of 20.1 with hit rate 15.1 despite stability being defined as the fraction of valid candidates that are stable and consistently being no larger than hit rate in Table 2.

Novelty appears limited to combining familiar LLM-guided evolutionary search, memory buffers, heuristic chemical rules, and existing property predictors. The paper does not isolate a technically novel optimization method, and several rule examples are vague or inappropriate for periodic inorganic crystals.

Reproducibility is insufficient: the code link is blank, complete scoring details and task weights are absent, API matching and similarity criteria are unspecified, seed populations and deduplication are unclear, candidate/iteration counts are inconsistent, and random seeds and run-level results are not reported.

The qualitative novelty analysis equates absence from Materials Project with genuine discovery. This can instead indicate hallucinated or invalid structures. Even highlighted examples are weakly vetted—for example, CaZnSi and MgZnSi are called “oxides” despite containing no oxygen—and none receives independent computational validation.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: multi-objective materials design under practical property constraints. Combining LLM generation, domain heuristics, memory, and island-based search is intuitively motivated.
The attempted empirical scope is broad, covering 14 application-oriented tasks, two LLM backbones, several generative and LLM baselines, and multiple evaluation views.
The paper includes component comparisons for memory, evolutionary operators, chemistry-informed rules, and surrogate prediction, alongside qualitative search-dynamics analyses.
The presentation is generally easy to follow, and the appendices provide an example prompt, heuristic rules, task descriptions, and nominal surrogate checkpoints.
weaknesses: The central discovery and synthesizability claims lack independent validation. Candidates are optimized and declared successful using the same pretrained surrogates, without DFT recalculation, structural relaxation, uncertainty analysis, synthesis assessment, or experiments. This creates a severe risk of exploiting surrogate errors on out-of-distribution, LLM-generated structures.

The paper equates predicted formation energy or energy above hull with synthesizability and describes sampled solutions as globally or truly Pareto-optimal. Thermodynamic predictions alone do not establish synthesizability, and a sampled surrogate-evaluated frontier cannot establish global optimality.

The benchmark is internally inconsistent. The main table and appendix give substantially different constraints for photovoltaic absorbers, hard coatings, and aerospace materials. The text says every task enforces thermodynamic stability, while the table omits stability constraints for many tasks. It is unclear what was actually evaluated.

Core details are missing or contradictory. The normalized reward function is undefined; weights are variously described as equal, lower for hull stability, and curated using domain heuristics. The failure-memory definition also conflicts with the algorithm, while candidate counts, iteration counts, and batch size do not reconcile clearly.

The evaluation lacks statistical and reproducibility support: no repeated trials, error bars, significance tests, seeds, complete prompts, generated candidate lists, or executable code are provided, and the title-page code field is blank.

The baseline comparison is poorly controlled. Default unconditional or differently conditioned generators are compared with an adaptive task-specific optimizer; allocating more samples does not make hit-rate percentages comparable. The treatment of G-SchNet as a periodic crystal generator and the baseline adaptations are inadequately justified.

The oracle mixes database values for known materials with surrogate estimates for novel ones, but matching thresholds, deduplication, and leakage controls are unspecified. Absence from Materials Project is treated as evidence of novelty and reduced memorization, although it establishes neither training-data novelty nor structural uniqueness.

Reported results contain unresolved inconsistencies. In one ablation, stability exceeds hit rate despite stability being defined as valid-and-stable candidates. The same SAW/BAW trajectory is described as reaching both roughly 46% and over 80% validity. Metric denominators and the validity procedure are unclear.

Chemical and structural validity are asserted but not demonstrated. There are no reported symmetry, interatomic-distance, charge-neutrality, oxidation-state, or relaxation checks. The qualitative discussion also calls CaZnSi and MgZnSi oxides even though the displayed formulas contain no oxygen.

The ablations cover only four tasks under constraints relaxed by 20%, so they do not directly explain the headline 14-task results. The surrogate ablation primarily shows that removing the mechanism used to score novel candidates removes the optimization signal; it does not validate discovered materials.

Overall, the attractive framework idea is overwhelmed by a circular, inconsistent evaluation that does not support the main claims of stable, synthesizable, real-world materials discovery. These are fundamental technical problems.

Reports substantial improvements in hit rate and predicted stability, alongside useful analyses of convergence, Pareto trade-offs, memorization, and system components.
The manuscript is generally well organized, and the appendices provide helpful descriptions of prompts, design rules, and predictor mappings.

Baseline fairness is not established: default unconditional crystal generators lack LLEMA's task conditioning, database-seeded memory, iterative oracle feedback, and domain rules. Giving them more samples does not resolve this capability mismatch.

Key evaluation details are missing, including structural-validity filtering, precise metric denominators, repeated-run statistics, uncertainty estimates, similarity-matching criteria, and surrogate accuracy on the generated-material distribution.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: multi-objective materials discovery under property and stability constraints.
Presents a coherent modular framework combining LLM generation, evolutionary memory, chemistry-inspired operators, and surrogate property prediction.

The empirical study is broad in surface coverage, spanning 14 tasks, two principal LLM backbones, several generative and LLM baselines, component ablations, prompt variations, model scales, and noise tests.
The paper is generally well organized, and the main algorithm, benchmark constraints, prompts, and surrogate checkpoints are described in useful detail.
weaknesses: The central evaluation is not independently reliable: surrogate models both guide the search and determine the headline hit-rate and stability results, creating substantial optimizer's-bias risk. LLEMA can exploit surrogate errors, so superior surrogate scores do not establish superior physical materials.

The claimed DFT validation is critically under-specified and internally unconvincing. Reporting only that Quantum ESPRESSO was run with 'default parameters' omits structures and relaxation protocols, exchange-correlation functional, pseudopotentials, cutoffs, k-point meshes, convergence criteria, magnetic treatment, and elemental reference energies. Energy above hull additionally requires consistent calculations of competing phases, while dielectric and piezoelectric properties require specialized DFPT workflows. Consequently, the reported 96–99% validity rates cannot be assessed or reproduced.

The DFT results do not report candidate-level values, surrogate-versus-DFT errors, task/property sample counts, selection protocol, uncertainty, failure cases, or baseline candidates. Table 9's per-property percentages are also not reconciled with the statement that 144/150 multi-constraint candidates pass. This does not substantiate the paper's strong claims of physical correctness.

The baselines are not convincingly fair. MatterGen is sampled from its base checkpoint rather than using its property-conditioning capabilities; G-SchNet is primarily a molecular generator; several methods are run with default settings and adapted post hoc; and the closest cited LLM evolutionary crystal-search method, MatLLMSearch, is not evaluated. Generation and compute budgets are also unclear and unequal.

The benchmark is described as realistic, but several tasks omit their defining physical objectives: solid electrolytes lack ionic conductivity, hard coatings lack hardness, acoustic substrates lack electromechanical coupling, and photovoltaics lack optical/transport properties. Some thresholds are overly permissive or physically questionable, most notably an aerospace energy-above-hull allowance of 5 eV/atom, which is incompatible with a meaningful stability requirement.

The manuscript conflates thermodynamic stability with synthesizability and real-world plausibility. Predicted low energy above hull alone does not establish kinetic accessibility, structural stability, manufacturability, or synthesis feasibility, and no experimental or synthesis-path validation is supplied.

Crystallographic validity is inadequately evaluated. The paper does not report rates for parseable CIFs, interatomic clashes, charge neutrality, oxidation-state consistency, symmetry, structural relaxation, or dynamic stability, despite claiming structurally accurate and physically realizable outputs.

The multi-objective contribution is technically weak: most tasks are feasibility filtering problems, the optimization uses a simple weighted sum with equal weights, and Pareto analysis is shown for only two tasks without hypervolume or coverage metrics. Claims of a 'globally optimal' or 'true' Pareto frontier are unsupported because only finite generated samples are compared.

Novelty and discovery are overstated. Absence from the Materials Project is treated as non-memorization or novelty, but it neither rules out presence in other databases/literature nor establishes that an LLM-generated structure is valid. The anecdotal candidate discussion includes ambiguous or inconsistent descriptions, such as calling CaZnSi and MgZnSi 'oxides' despite the displayed formulas containing no oxygen.

The experiments lack repeated runs, confidence intervals, statistical tests, and sensitivity analyses for key search hyperparameters beyond island count. Several ablations use relaxed constraints, fewer iterations, and only four tasks, limiting their relevance to the main results.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the headline claims: the code and dataset fields are blank, complete candidate structures and scores are not released in the manuscript, proprietary-model versioning is vague, and essential oracle and DFT implementation details are absent.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: iterative, multi-property materials design that combines LLM proposals with structured crystal representations and external property predictors.
LLEMA is conceptually easy to follow, and the success/failure memories, multi-island search, and chemistry-inspired operators form a coherent pipeline.
The evaluation spans 14 tasks and two primary LLM backbones, with additional studies of rules, memory, island count, model scale, prompt variation, surrogate noise, efficiency, and diversity.
The authors attempt higher-fidelity validation of generated candidates using DFT rather than relying exclusively on surrogate scores.
The manuscript is generally readable, and the appendix supplies prompts, property-to-surrogate mappings, scoring equations, and the list of generation rules.
weaknesses: The central claims of synthesizability and physical validity are not adequately supported. Low predicted formation energy or energy above hull is not equivalent to synthesizability, and the paper reports no synthesis-route analysis, structural relaxation results, dynamical stability, or experimental validation.

The reported DFT validation is not reproducible or technically credible as described. Quantum ESPRESSO calculations are said to use “default parameters,” without pseudopotentials, exchange-correlation functional, cutoffs, k-point meshes, convergence criteria, spin treatment, structural relaxation, or procedures for formation energy, convex-hull energy, band gap, and piezoelectric properties. The extraordinary 94–96% constraint-satisfaction rates therefore cannot be assessed.

Generated CIF quality is a critical missing evaluation. There are no standard structural-validity measures, interatomic-distance checks, charge-neutrality checks, relaxation success rates, symmetry analyses, or comparisons between generated and relaxed structures. Feeding arbitrary LLM-generated coordinates into graph predictors does not establish that the structures are physically meaningful.

The evaluation is vulnerable to surrogate exploitation: LLEMA optimizes the same pretrained predictors subsequently used to declare hits. There is no systematic out-of-distribution error analysis, uncertainty calibration, or equally sampled DFT comparison of LLEMA and baseline candidates.

Baseline comparisons are not convincingly fair. Several generative models are sampled from default or base checkpoints without task-specific conditioning, whereas LLEMA receives explicit constraints and iterative oracle feedback. MatLLMSearch, an especially close evolutionary LLM method cited by the paper, is not evaluated. Candidate budgets and compute matching are also unclear and seemingly inconsistent with the claim that non-LLM methods receive about ten times more generations.

The benchmark is presented as realistic and industrially relevant, but several tasks omit their defining physical quantities: solid electrolytes have no ionic-conductivity constraint, transparent conductors use no direct optical-transparency measure, and mechanical applicability is reduced to a few moduli. The aerospace stability threshold of energy above hull at most 5 eV/atom is physically implausibly loose and conflicts with the paper’s general 0.1 eV/atom stability definition.

Many tasks are feasibility filtering problems rather than well-defined multi-objective optimization problems. The paper mainly reports threshold hit rates, while Pareto quality is shown qualitatively for only two tasks without hypervolume, coverage, or other quantitative Pareto metrics. Claims of finding the “true” or “globally optimal” Pareto frontier are unjustified in an open chemical search space evaluated by approximate surrogates.

Statistical rigor is insufficient. Results lack independent runs, confidence intervals, variance estimates, significance tests, and clear seed information despite stochastic LLM sampling and evolutionary search. Small differences and robustness claims consequently cannot be interpreted reliably.

The novelty assessment is weak. The framework largely combines established LLM-guided evolutionary search, memories, heuristic chemical substitutions, and pretrained property predictors; its distinction from closely related materials-search systems is asserted more than experimentally demonstrated.

The chemical rules are prompt heuristics rather than enforced constraints, and several—surface functionalization, functional-group substitution, and retrosynthesis—do not naturally produce valid bulk inorganic crystals. No per-rule ablation or rule-compliance measurement is provided.

Some qualitative evidence raises correctness concerns: CaZnSi and MgZnSi are described as “oxides” although the displayed formulas contain no oxygen, and novelty is inferred largely from absence in the Materials Project rather than from rigorous structure matching or broader database searches.

The memorization and diversity analyses are underdefined. It is unclear whether Materials Project overlap is measured by formula, exact structure, or structural similarity, while periodic-table coverage and elemental overlap are weak proxies for meaningful compositional or structural diversity.

The noise experiment injects the same absolute standard deviation into properties with very different units and scales, then evaluates robustness using elemental overlap; this does not provide a meaningful test of sensitivity to realistic surrogate uncertainty.

Reproducibility is poor: the manuscript leaves the code and dataset fields blank, does not release generated structures or DFT inputs, and omits important API, model-checkpoint, preprocessing, deduplication, and failure-handling details. Overall, the empirical breadth does not compensate for the invalid or insufficiently documented validation of the paper’s main scientific claims.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem and proposes an appealing integration of LLM generation, chemistry-informed operators, success/failure memory, multi-island search, and surrogate property prediction.

The evaluation spans 14 application-oriented, multi-constraint tasks and compares against both crystal generative models and LLM-based methods. The reported hit-rate improvements are often substantial across two LLM backbones.
The paper includes useful component analyses covering evolutionary guidance, island count, prompt variation, model scale, surrogate removal, noise, memorization, diversity, and computational cost.
The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with intuitive figures and explicit descriptions of the scoring rules, prompts, surrogate checkpoints, and chemical operators.
weaknesses: The principal evaluation is not independent: the same surrogate-assisted oracle guides the search and determines hit rate and stability. An optimizer can exploit surrogate errors, so these metrics do not by themselves establish that the generated materials possess the claimed properties.

The purported DFT validation is insufficiently specified to resolve this issue. The paper states that Quantum ESPRESSO was run with “default parameters,” but omits pseudopotentials, exchange-correlation functional, cutoffs, k-point grids, structural relaxation, convergence criteria, spin treatment, and property-specific workflows. Energy above hull requires consistent calculations of competing phases, while piezoelectric and dielectric properties require specialized calculations. Reporting only threshold agreement percentages, without errors, candidate-level results, sample counts per property, or reproducible inputs, does not substantiate the remarkable 94–96% overall success claims.

Baseline fairness and statistical reliability are unclear. Candidate budgets are not transparently matched, LLEMA uses iterative task feedback whereas several generative baselines appear to use unconditional base checkpoints followed by screening, and the closely related MatLLMSearch is discussed but not evaluated. No repeated runs, uncertainty intervals, or significance tests are reported despite stochastic LLM generation.

The multi-objective claims are overstated. The method itself uses a weighted scalar score plus feasibility filtering, while Pareto quality is shown visually for only two tasks without hypervolume, coverage, or diversity metrics. A frontier over sampled candidates cannot be called the “true,” “globally optimal” Pareto frontier.

Synthesizability and experimental realizability are repeatedly claimed but are reduced largely to surrogate-predicted thermodynamic stability. There is no synthesis-route assessment or experimental validation, and some benchmark constraints are questionable—for example, an aerospace energy-above-hull threshold of 5 eV/atom is far too permissive to indicate stability.

Several evaluation definitions and results are internally unclear. Table 4 reports stability exceeding hit rate for one method even though stability is described as the fraction of valid candidates that are also stable; exact/similarity database matching is unspecified; conductivity inferred from Seebeck coefficient and power factor lacks temperature, doping, and unit details; and structural validity checks for generated CIFs are not rigorously documented.

Reproducibility is below the expected standard: the code and dataset links are blank, main-run iteration and total-candidate accounting are ambiguous, random seeds and repeat protocols are absent, and the released artifacts needed to reproduce the DFT verification are not provided. These issues affect the paper’s central empirical claims rather than constituting minor omissions.
